channel.title: RetroMac
channel.description: Most recent changes with links to updates.

item.title: Version 3.1
item.description:
RetroMac 3.1

New

  • New theme: KDE 1.0. The K Desktop Environment of July 1998, from KDE's own sources: the panel along the bottom with the K menu, the window list, launchers that open the nearest Mac app, logout and lock, the four desktops One to Four with the four backgrounds KDE shipped, and the clock; the taskbar along the top with a button per window (a click brings it forward, the middle button iconifies, the right one opens the window menu); Qt's grey menus; KDE 1.0's original icons, with pictures in its style for today's apps; and kwm's shaded blue title bars on RetroMac's own windows. The K menu sorts your apps into KDE's groups, "All Applications" lists every one and "Run Command..." starts one by its name. The Mac menu bar hides while the theme is on, so the taskbar holds the top edge as it did on a KDE screen.
  • New theme: Atari TOS 4.04. The colour GEM desktop of the Falcon030 (1993): the white menu bar with Desk, File, View and Options whose menus open as the pointer reaches them, the light blue desktop with the startup disk as drive C, TRASH in the bottom left corner and the original icons from the Falcon's Language Disk, each with its selected picture. APPS, a drive added by RetroMac, opens a GEM window with every Mac app, as icons or as text, sorted by name or type, with scroll arrows, sliders and a size box. Install Application puts an app on the desktop without copying it; what you drop on TRASH goes to the Mac's own trash. While a Mac app is in front, its own menus are back. The desktop comes furnished as a Falcon owner's did: FLOPPY DISK A (which, a Mac having no floppy drive, answers that it is not responding), GAMES with the joystick opening RetroMac's games, and down the right edge TextEdit with the pencil, Preview with the drawing hand, Documents, Utilities with the pliers and the README.
  • New theme: OS X Mavericks. 10.9 of 2013, built on the Mountain Lion theme: the Mavericks wave as the desktop, an empty desktop as after a fresh install, the glass dock with its reflections, the thin dark divider that leans with the shelf, today's date on the Calendar icon even while Calendar is closed, the new Maps and iBooks icons of 10.9, iTunes 11's deep blue icon, the lighter 10.9 title bar with its regular-weight title on RetroMac's own windows and widgets, 10.8's Apple menu, About This Mac, pointers and crash screen, Mission Control as the switcher, and a Read Me with the story of the first free OS X.
  • Today's date on the Calendar icon in Tiger, Snow Leopard and Mountain Lion. As in the originals: Snow Leopard and Mountain Lion show it at all times, as every Mac OS X since 10.5 did; Tiger only while Calendar is running and JUL 17 otherwise, as iCal did up to 10.4.
  • Tiger's dock badges in Mail's look. Before 10.5 the Dock drew no badges; apps painted the red dot into their own icons the way Mail did, so Tiger now shows that brighter dot instead of the deeper red pill the Dock itself drew from Leopard to Mavericks.
  • Option-click the green button for full screen. Under the Mac themes the green button zooms the window, as it did before Lion; with Option held it now puts the app into macOS full screen.

item.title: Version 3.0.8
item.description:
RetroMac 3.0.8

New

  • New theme: Windows 2000 Professional. The plain blue-grey desktop (#3A6EA5) with My Documents, My Computer, My Network Places, the Recycle Bin and Internet Explorer, the grey #D4D0C8 taskbar, and 2000's own Start menu: Windows Update, Programs, Documents, Settings, Search (files, the Internet, people), Help, Run… and Shut Down…, under the black and blue "Windows 2000 Professional" banner. Folders open in the Explorer.
  • The Windows themes have their Explorer. Windows 95 to 7 open folders, My Computer and My Documents in a Windows Explorer of their own: the Mac's disks as C:, D:…, Large Icons, List and Details, an address bar that takes Windows paths, Windows 98's folder panel or XP's task pane, cut, copy and paste (with the Finder too), drag and drop, rename in place, the Recycle Bin and Undo. Windows 95 to 2000 show Windows 2000's own icons (folders, drives, CD-ROM, network drive, Control Panel, text, sound, video, picture and web files) in 8 pt Tahoma with Windows 98's own toolbar (grey, coloured under the pointer), XP to 7 show XP's icons and XP's toolbar (Back, Forward, Up, Views), the title bar is the one the theme draws on every other window (the theme's colours, height and buttons, XP's caption buttons), and the Programs icon on the desktop opens Program Files in it. The Finder's places in the Start menu and on Quick Launch are Windows Explorer there (C:\ on 95 to Me and NT, My Documents from 2000 on), and every Explorer window has its button on the taskbar: its minimise button puts it there, a click brings it back. Notepad, Calculator and XP's Task Manager get theirs too (their minimise used to close them), and Calculator gets the minimise box it lacked, with calc.exe's greyed maximise.
  • Start ▸ Run… is the Run dialog. It opens what you type: notepad, calc, cmd, control, taskmgr or explorer, a web address, a path, or any app by name, and it remembers the last ten.
  • File windows that never lose a file, with Undo. Tiger's Finder, the Amiga drawers and the Explorer copy without writing over anything, put a replaced item in the Trash, ask before replacing, show the progress of long copies, and ⌘Z takes any of it back, the Trash included. Tiger's Finder learns ⌘C, ⌘V and ⌥⌘V.
  • Notepad writes in its own font again. Windows 95 to 2000 in a Fixedsys-like VGA face (PxPlus IBM VGA 8x16), XP to 7 in Lucida Console where installed, not Courier New.
  • Notepad keeps your files as they were. It saves with the file's own line endings, byte-order mark and encoding, refuses binary and very large files with a message, never half-writes a file, and under the Windows themes opens and saves through Windows dialogs. The file operations, the Run dialog's search and the text files are adapted from retro98 by matheushchaves (MIT).

item.title: Version 3.0.7
item.description:
RetroMac 3.0.7

New

  • Amiga Workbench 4.1, the AmigaOne of 2008. The theme now follows AmigaOS 4.1 as it stood after a fresh install. Its windows get AmigaOS's own title bars, blue in front and silver behind, with the closer on the left and depth, zoom and iconify on the right; the depth gadget sends the front window behind all the windows it covers. The Workbench screen bar runs along the top with the free memory; its screen-depth gadget puts the other programs away to show the Workbench, and brings them back. Hold the right mouse button for the Workbench, Window, Icons and Tools menus. The AmiDock sits at the bottom right with each name under its icon; the Mac's apps take their 2008 Amiga counterparts where there was one (Safari as IBrowse, Mail as YAM, Music as PlayCD, QuickTime as DvPlayer, Terminal as Shell), the rest Workbench-style pictures. The volumes are on the left: System, Work and a private RAM Disk. Drawers open in windows of their own, showing only objects with an icon (or all files), with Snapshot and AmigaOS 4 .info pictures. With Boot Phases on Firmware, the AmigaOne's U-Boot comes first, with today's date, then the AmigaOS 4.1 boot screen. The Tools menu holds WBPattern (the wallpapers, among them djnick's Amiga Abstract and Andreas Argirakis's Pairing Joysticks from amiga-look.org), New shortcut and the Clock, Calculator, Notepad and CPU Monitor in Workbench windows; the mouse pointers are levellord's AmigaOS 4 set (CC BY-SA 4.0). The AmiDock carries three Dockies: an analog clock, a CPU load graph in Ranger's manner and WinBar, the list of open windows, minimised ones included. The AmiDock starts as a fresh install had it (NotePad, Shell, MultiView, UnArc and Help), with the Extras, Internet and Players sub-docks opening in a column above their tile; running programs get no tile of their own, and an iconified window becomes an icon on the Workbench. The dockbar at the dock's end holds its menu; other apps' windows wear the blue frame only in front; and the Workbench menu can switch the screen title to the machine in one line, as the Final Edition shows it. Every picture is redrawn for RetroMac, including a reconstruction of the 2008 backdrop, and the type is DejaVu Sans, as on OS 4.1.

item.title: Version 3.0.6
item.description:
RetroMac 3.0.6

New

  • New theme: Mac OS X 10.4 Tiger. Aqua Blue, the frosted dock without 10.0's pinstripes (white at about 42 %, black triangles under running apps), the blue Aqua Apple, and brushed metal across the title bars where Cheetah has pinstripes, with the title embossed in white. Ten of Tiger's desktop pictures: Aqua Blue and Aqua Graphite, Lotus, Leaf Curl, the tiger's fur, the Classic, Jaguar and Panther Aqua Blues, Clown Fish and Stones. Dashboard sits on the desktop, Exposé answers the window switcher, the Aqua pointers and the red dock badges come along. The menu bar is 10.4's plain white one.
  • Tiger's Finder. The desktop's Macintosh HD and Applications open a Finder of RetroMac's own: brushed metal, Back and Forward, icon, list and column views (⌘1, ⌘2, ⌘3), the action menu, the sidebar of places, "9 items, 70.32 GB available" along the bottom. It works on the real files: a double-click opens a file in its app, Return renames, ⌘D duplicates, ⇧⌘N makes a folder, ⌘⌫ moves to the Mac's Trash (nothing is deleted outright), ⌘↑ goes up, ⌘↓ opens, folders fold open in the list. Its search field asks Spotlight.
  • Tiger's Spotlight. The blue magnifier in the menu bar drops the menu: the Top Hit, then Applications, Documents, Folders, Images and the rest, at most five each, from the Mac's own index. The arrows move, Return opens, Escape closes; Show All opens the results in the Finder. A search typed over never shows the results of the letters before. ⌘Space stays the Mac's.
  • Tiger's details, against 10.4 screenshots. About This Mac is 10.4's own: the small window with the smooth grey bar and faint pinstripes, the silver apple, "Mac OS X", Processor and Memory, 2005's copyright line. The Apple menu is 10.4's (About This Mac, Software Update…, Mac OS X Software…, Force Quit with the front app's name, Restart…, Shut Down…, Log Out with your name) in the white menu. The desktop's Clock, CPU, Notepad, Calculator and TV wear brushed metal, the TV window too. The dock's edge and divider are dark, a groove between two light lines, as on 10.4. Spotlight takes the rightmost place macOS gives an app. The Finder's toolbar has Tiger's glossy buttons (pale blue for the chosen view, grey arrows when there is nowhere to go), all three lights work, the sidebar selection is 10.4's blue, folders are paled to its light blue and the icon grid is roomier. The sidebar carries 10.4's own pictures (Network's globe, the disk, Desktop, the house, Applications, Documents, Movies, Music, Pictures) in 10.4's taller rows, Network first. The TV folder's toolbar is metal too.
  • The desktop companion comes back from the flyout. After Hide Assistant, the flyout's new Desktop Companion switch brings back the last one that was on (Clippy where "Match the theme" has no one), no trip to Settings.
  • Tips go by themselves. A Mac or RetroMac tip leaves after eight seconds, or at a click on it.
  • SETI@home's new icon in the Windows themes, one picture shared by all five.
  • Minimising lands in the theme's dock again under Mac OS X, Tiger, Snow Leopard and Mountain Lion. The Mac's own minimise aims at the hidden Mac Dock, whose icons sit elsewhere, and the window flew past the theme's dock to the left. A window minimised with the theme's yellow light or ⌘M now shrinks into its app's icon in the theme's dock, as Halloween's does.
  • Exposé's F11. A third Exposé shortcut (Settings ▸ Shortcuts, ⌃F11): every app out of the way and the desktop bare; again brings them back.
  • Tiger's start-up chime. On *Firmware → OS Boot → Desktop* Tiger strikes the Mac's F-sharp-major chord before the grey Apple, once. Synthesised, not a recording.
  • Built-in themes share their files. Tiger's app icons are Cheetah's (the same 10.4 set), its boot film is Snow Leopard's and six of its desktop pictures live in Cheetah and Snow Leopard: links inside the app, not copies. Aqua Blue, shared with Cheetah, is now 2880 pixels wide instead of 1920. A duplicated theme gets real copies, and an imported theme still cannot reach outside its own folder.
  • Desktop companion (Settings ▸ Desktop). One choice for the sheep and the Office assistants: Clippy and The Genius come with RetroMac; F1, Genie, Links, Merlin, Peedy, Rocky and Rover download when picked. *Match the theme* puts Clippy on the Windows themes and Rover on XP. The assistants also work without a theme. No AI: click one for the last ten texts you copied (in memory only, password fields stay out), a note with to-dos and the rest of today; it says when a meeting starts in ten minutes (with *Join* for its video link), when a reminder is due (*Done*, *Later*), when a download has finished, a disk is plugged in, the battery is low, the disk nearly full or the last Time Machine backup a week old. Tips are yours to pick: Mac tips for the app in front, RetroMac tips (with *Show me*), and, if you like, the start of English Wikipedia's article of the day with *Read more* — the only thing it fetches from the internet. It slips out from under the flyout button and back in when hidden; drag it anywhere, double-click to see its animations one by one, right-click for Animate!, another assistant or Hide. After five quiet minutes it falls asleep (Clippy curls up on his paper, Peedy yawns and nods off) and wakes at the next click or message. VoiceOver reads what it says; with Reduce Motion it stands still.
  • Themes by age. The menu bar's Themes menu and the flyout list each family youngest era first (Mountain Lion down to System 6, Windows 7 down to 3.1). The 100 % Apple and Windows themes wear the Apple or the Windows logo instead of 💯; Off moves to the bottom of the menu.
  • Quick Access in tabs. The flyout's eight slots become three rows of eight: Apple, Windows and Various, each its own. The slots you had go to their family's tab first, the rest of each family fills up behind them. "Edit Quick Access" sits beside RetroMac at the top; the Quick Access caption is gone.
  • Moving windows (Settings ▸ Themes, under the title bars): *As the era did*, *Outline* or *Whole window*. With *Outline* only a frame moves and the window follows when you let go; dragged by its own title bar, the bars and borders step aside until it stops, so nothing trails behind it.

Fixes

  • An imported theme whose icons folder is a link stays inside its own folder. The lookup followed the link before drawing the fence, so the fence moved with it.
  • A macOS update can no longer stop RetroMac from starting. The private WindowServer functions behind the window borders and title bars are now linked weakly: if one is gone, both features stay off (and say so in the log) instead of the app refusing to launch.
  • Windows moved down for their title bar always go back. The way back is kept on disk, kept while a window is minimised, and used at the next start after a crash, even if the bars are off by then.
  • The patch over the real traffic lights takes its colour from that window alone, not from whatever lay over it, and no longer blinks off each time it is retaken.
  • Smoother with many windows. Moves arriving in bursts are handled once per window, the borders and title bars share one window list, an app that does not answer holds up only its own windows, and the buttons and the room-making move no longer wait on the main thread.
  • VoiceOver keeps its place in Settings ▸ Sounds. The tab was rebuilt every two seconds, whether anything had changed or not, and VoiceOver lost the setting it was on. It now changes only when something it shows does.
  • VoiceOver reads the Sounds sliders' values, not their position: "Starts at" said 31 % for 35 % CPU load, "Run-on" a percentage for seconds. Each slider says its own value and unit.
  • The Sounds tab's switches are the ones of every other tab, and the fan chart is one element with a steady name and the current values as its value.

item.title: Version 3.0.5
item.description:
RetroMac 3.0.5

New

  • Boot Phases. The two boot-screen switches are now one slider with three stops (Settings ▸ Dock ▸ Behaviour and the Setup Assistant): *Desktop* switches a theme on straight away, *OS Boot → Desktop* plays its boot as before, *Firmware → OS Boot → Desktop* starts with the machine's firmware. Each theme can keep its own choice. A new install starts on Desktop; an existing one keeps what it had (boot screens on → OS Boot). VoiceOver and Reduce Motion go straight to the desktop.
  • A BIOS you can enter. The Windows themes start with their PC's firmware: AMIBIOS of 1992 for Windows 3.1, Award Modular BIOS v4.51PG for 95, 98 and Me, Phoenix - AwardBIOS v6.00PG for XP, Vista and 7. The POST counts this Mac's real memory and names its real processor and model, the Energy Star mark included. DEL (or the delete key) opens the CMOS setup: every page can be walked with the arrow keys and changed with PgUp/PgDn or +/-, F10 saves. Two settings do something: *Quick Power On Self Test* shortens the POST, *Boot Up Floppy Seek* makes the floppy drive seek (with the drive sounds on). The rest are kept as set, as CMOS kept them. The key that enters the setup can be chosen (Settings ▸ Dock ▸ Behaviour): DEL, which a Mac's delete key (⌫) also is, or F1, F2 or F10, and the POST names the one chosen.
  • New theme: Windows NT 4.0, the Workstation edition (Build 1381, 1996, the shell before IE4's Desktop Update). 95's chrome and taskbar without Quick Launch; the desktop of a fresh install (My Computer, Network Neighborhood, Inbox, Internet Explorer, Recycle Bin, My Briefcase); the Start menu with NT's banner and program groups, whose Administrative Tools open the Mac's own (Disk Administrator is Disk Utility, Event Viewer the Console, Performance Monitor the Activity Monitor). On *Firmware* it boots through an Award BIOS, the OS Loader V4.0 menu, NTDETECT, the blue kernel screen with this Mac's processors and memory, then NT's start-up screen on teal and the desktop: no log-on box, nothing asks for a password. The wallpaper centres NT's start-up artwork on teal #058182.
  • All Programs in the Windows Start menus. A new folder at the top of Programs lists every app on the Mac, sorted into Communication, Design, Games, Multimedia, Office, Online and System Tools by the app's own App Store category (and a list of well-known apps that have none, like the browsers); the rest follows below the folders. Everything else in the menu stays where it was.
  • Windows NT 4.0's program groups are filled. Accessories holds Calculator, Clock, Imaging, Notepad, Paint and WordPad, with Games (Minesweeper, Solitaire) and Multimedia (CD Player, Media Player, Sound Recorder, Volume Control); Administrative Tools adds Command Prompt and User Manager; Startup lists what the Mac opens at login.

Fixes

  • Folders inside the Start menu's flyouts open. A folder in a flyout (All Programs ▸ Office, Accessories ▸ Games) showed its arrow and did nothing; it now opens its own flyout beside it, on hover, on a click or with the arrow keys.
  • No desktop through the corners under a theme's title bar. A window opened before the bars went on keeps macOS's rounded corners until its app restarts, and under the square bar the desktop showed through them. A band in the window's own colour now sits behind the top of every barred window: the window hides it, except in those corners.
  • A click on a taskbar button brings its window to the front again. The window came up inside its app but stayed behind the front one: the window server's front-process call RetroMac used reports success on macOS 27.3 and changes nothing. The app is now brought to the front through Accessibility as well.
  • Settings ▸ Dock: the theme dropdown picks, "Show theme now" switches. Picking a theme no longer switches the Mac to it on the spot; the settings below it show the picked theme, and "Show theme now" (formerly "Show dock now", which with a theme on did nothing visible) turns it on. The button greys out while the picked theme is the one running.
  • Mac OS 9.2 Classic's desktop icons are as large as Mac OS 9 (authentic)'s: 32 points instead of the dock's 28.
  • The menu-bar strip in the Mac themes' wallpaper reaches every display. Coming from a theme that hides the menu bar (the Windows ones), a display without a notch kept the plain wallpaper: macOS still reported no menu bar there when the picture was painted. RetroMac now reads the bar from the window server and paints again once the bar is back.
  • Mountain Lion keeps Applications in the dock again, as a grid stack next to Downloads.
  • Snow Leopard's and Mountain Lion's traffic lights sit a point higher, level with the title; on the real buttons' centres the gel orbs looked as if they hung low.
  • Windows 95 shows the MS-DOS Prompt icon of Windows 98, as Windows NT 4.0 now does.
  • A boot screen left over from a quick theme switch no longer touches the next one. The first switch's video deadline could stop the second one's video and run its switch.
  • A theme's boot video stays inside the theme, like every other file it names.

item.title: Version 2.2
item.description:
RetroMac 2.2: please update manually, one time

This release includes a technical change to how updates are delivered, so your copy can’t install it automatically. Please download 2.2 from the button below and drag it into your Applications folder, just this once. After that, automatic updates work as normal again.

  • Authentic Mac System 6: true 1-bit black & white theme.
  • Warcraft I + II: play them natively with your own game data.
  • Mac OS X boot animation for the Mac OS X and Snow Leopard themes.
  • Clearer Pro unlocks and assorted polish.
